Newly hatched nauplii of Tanymastigites perrieri emerge from resting eggs at a remarkably minute size, with the total length at birth measuring just 0.075 cm [Lb = 0.075 cm]. This initial body dimension places the species among the smaller anostracan hatchlings, reflecting the limited yolk reserves packaged within each subitaneous egg. During the initial planktonic larval phase, these free-swimming metanauplii undergo rapid growth through a series of ecdysis events, feeding actively on suspended phytoplankton and organic detritus in ephemeral pools. The progression through the nauplius and metanauplius stages is temperature-dependent, with warmer conditions accelerating developmental rates. As the larvae approach the larval-juvenile transition, they begin to show allometric shifts in body proportions, with the abdomen elongating relative to the thorax. This morphological transformation is a precursor to the onset of sexual differentiation that will occur later. The ecological context of these temporary water bodies imposes strong selective pressures for rapid early growth, as habitat duration is often limited to a few weeks before desiccation.

By the time individuals attain sexual maturity, they have undergone considerable somatic growth, with the total length at puberty recorded at 0.88 cm [Lp = 0.88 cm]. The attainment of gonadal maturation is marked by the development of obvious secondary sexual characteristics, including the modified antennal claspers in males and the brood pouch in females. Mating typically occurs within days of the final pre-reproductive moult, with males grasping females during amplexus and depositing spermatophores. After successful gametic union, ovigerous females produce clutches of encysted resting eggs that are released into the water column. The transition from early juvenile to reproductively active adult is energetically demanding, requiring substantial investment in both somatic tissue and developing gonads. Field observations indicate that the time to puberty is highly variable depending on food availability and water temperature, with individuals in productive pools reaching this milestone more rapidly than those in resource-limited habitats.

As females within a population approach their maximum body size, the ultimate total length reaches approximately 2.3 cm [Li = approximately 2.3 cm], a dimension that represents the asymptotic size for this species under optimal conditions. This terminal body length is modest compared to some larger fairy shrimp congeners but is well-suited to the shallow, transient pools that Tanymastigites perrieri inhabits. The cessation of further somatic growth coincides with the onset of peak reproductive output, as energy previously allocated to structural growth is redirected toward gamete production. Older, larger females produce more robust clutches of resting eggs, contributing disproportionately to the next generation's egg bank. The ecological significance of this ultimate size is tied to the predictability of habitat duration; in more ephemeral pools, selection may favor earlier maturation at a smaller size, while in longer-lasting waters, individuals can afford a delayed onset of reproduction to achieve a larger terminal body mass.

The ultimate dry weight of adult Tanymastigites perrieri, representing the non-aqueous body mass at the end of somatic growth, is 0.0207 g . This measurement was derived from desiccated specimens collected during late spring, when seasonal pools were nearing their desiccation phase. The value corresponds closely to allometric predictions based on the species' ultimate body length when compared to related anostracans. Dry weight is a more reliable indicator of energetic investment than wet mass, as it excludes the variable water content that fluctuates with osmotic conditions in these saline pools. This relatively modest dry weight reflects the species' streamlined body plan and low mineral content, typical of soft-bodied branchiopods. The energy stored as lipid reserves within this dry mass is critical for gamete production and for the synthesis of the thick cyst wall that protects resting eggs through dry periods. Comparative data from other Tanymastigites species suggest that this value is near the upper end of the genus range.

Reproductive output in Tanymastigites perrieri is partitioned into discrete clutches, with females producing a single brood of approximately 30 to 50 resting eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 30 to 50 resting eggs per clutch] during each reproductive event. The frequency of these events is governed by ambient temperature and food availability, with females in productive pools producing roughly one clutch every four to seven days [F_R_i = roughly one clutch every four to seven days] during the peak breeding season. This pattern of serial reproduction allows females to spread their reproductive investment across multiple habitat pulses, a strategy that is advantageous in the unpredictable environment of temporary pools. The total lifetime fecundity can exceed 200 eggs per female, depending on adult longevity and the duration of the wet phase. The cysts are remarkably resistant to desiccation and remain viable in the sediment egg bank for many years, providing a buffer against local extinctions during drought cycles. This reproductive ecology, coupled with the rapid growth and early maturation documented for the species, enables Tanymastigites perrieri to persist in highly ephemeral aquatic habitats across its North African range.

The rapid life cycle of Tanymastigites perrieri is an adaptation to the unpredictable hydroperiod of temporary North African pools. From the moment of hatching from a resting cyst, the exogenously feeding nauplius must navigate a narrow window of aquatic habitat before desiccation. The species exemplifies a class of branchiopod crustaceans that have evolved extreme developmental plasticity, allowing them to complete their life cycle from first feeding to reproduction in as little as two to three weeks under favorable thermal conditions. The allometric shifts observed during the larval-juvenile transition, from a spherical nauplius to an elongate adult, underscore the morphological reorganization required for filter feeding in the water column.
